claim: The T-cell receptor complex contains six immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) from CD3 chains.
source: The T-cell receptor complex contains six immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) from CD3 chains that, when phosphorylated, bind to the tSH2 domain of ZAP70 (ZtSH2).
evidence: Stated in Figure 1 caption and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the TCR complex structure with ITAMs.

claim: ITAMs from CD3 chains, when phosphorylated, bind to the tSH2 domain of ZAP70 (ZtSH2).
source: The T-cell receptor complex contains six immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) from CD3 chains that, when phosphorylated, bind to the tSH2 domain of ZAP70 (ZtSH2).
evidence: Stated in Figure 1 caption and illustrated in Figure 1A; this is established knowledge about TCR signaling.

claim: Three repeats of CD3 ITAMs were appended to the C-terminus of EGFR to create the EGFR pYtag.
source: Three repeats of CD3 ITAMs were appended to the C-terminus of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol was assessed.
evidence: Described in Figure 1B caption and illustrated in the schematic showing EGFR-ITAM-FusionRed construct.

claim: NIH3T3 cells expressing EGFR pYtag (CD3ε variant) exhibit clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol upon EGF treatment.
source: Timelapse images of NIH3T3 cells expressing EGFR pYtag (CD3ε variant), treated first with EGF (100 ng/mL) and then with gefitinib (10 µM).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C timelapse images demonstrating ZtSH2 redistribution from cytosol to membrane after EGF treatment.

claim: Gefitinib treatment reverses ZtSH2 clearance from the cytosol in EGFR pYtag-expressing cells.
source: Clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol was quickly reversed by treatment with gefitinib, an inhibitor of EGFR kinase activity, indicating that ZtSH2 can serve as a rapid, reversible reporter of EGFR activation (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C timelapse and quantified in Figure 1D-E showing reversal of ZtSH2 clearance after gefitinib addition.

claim: Cells lacking EGFR or expressing ITAM-less EGFR exhibit no change in ZtSH2 localization in response to EGF or gefitinib treatment.
source: Cells lacking EGFR or expressing an ITAM-less EGFR-FusionRed exhibited no change in ZtSH2 localization in response to treatment with EGF or gefitinib (Figure 1D and E), demonstrating that the ZtSH2 reporter responds specifically to the activation of an ITAM-labeled RTK.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D-E where control conditions show no ZtSH2 clearance, demonstrating specificity of the pYtag system.

claim: All six tested ITAMs from CD3γ, CD3δ, CD3ε, and CD3ζ chains can function as biosensors of RTK activity.
source: Although all six ITAMs that we tested appear capable of functioning as biosensors of RTK activity, we chose to focus on the CD3ε ITAM for all subsequent experiments due to its reported selectivity for ZtSH2 over other phosphotyrosine-binding domains (Osman et al., 1995; Ravichandran et al., 1993; Love and Hayes, 2010).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1D-E showing ZtSH2 clearance for all six ITAM variants tested, with citations supporting CD3ε selectivity.

claim: CD3ε ITAM was selected for subsequent experiments due to its reported selectivity for ZtSH2 over other phosphotyrosine-binding domains.
source: Although all six ITAMs that we tested appear capable of functioning as biosensors of RTK activity, we chose to focus on the CD3ε ITAM for all subsequent experiments due to its reported selectivity for ZtSH2 over other phosphotyrosine-binding domains (Osman et al., 1995; Ravichandran et al., 1993; Love and Hayes, 2010).
evidence: Stated explicitly with supporting citations from literature.

claim: Grb2 localizes to the membrane in both ITAM-tagged and ITAM-less EGFR cells upon EGF stimulation.
source: Stimulating these cells with EGF revealed that Grb2 localized to the membrane in both ITAM-tagged and ITAM-less EGFR cells, whereas ZtSH2 only showed membrane recruitment in the ITAM-tagged context (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E showing Grb2 membrane localization regardless of ITAM presence.

claim: ZtSH2 only shows membrane recruitment in ITAM-tagged EGFR cells, not in ITAM-less EGFR cells.
source: Stimulating these cells with EGF revealed that Grb2 localized to the membrane in both ITAM-tagged and ITAM-less EGFR cells, whereas ZtSH2 only showed membrane recruitment in the ITAM-tagged context (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E showing ZtSH2 specificity for ITAM-tagged receptors.

claim: EGFR, Erk, and Akt are phosphorylated at similar levels in cells expressing EGFR-FusionRed or EGFR pYtag after EGF stimulation.
source: We found that EGFR, Erk, and Akt were phosphorylated at similar levels in the two cell lines (Figure 1G), suggesting that ITAM phosphorylation and ZtSH2 recruitment do not interfere with signaling downstream of EGFR.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1F-G immunoblots and quantification demonstrating similar phosphorylation levels between control and pYtag-expressing cells.

claim: ITAM phosphorylation and ZtSH2 recruitment do not interfere with signaling downstream of EGFR.
source: We found that EGFR, Erk, and Akt were phosphorylated at similar levels in the two cell lines (Figure 1G), suggesting that ITAM phosphorylation and ZtSH2 recruitment do not interfere with signaling downstream of EGFR.
evidence: Inferred from similar phosphorylation levels shown in Figure 1F-G between control and pYtag-expressing cells.

claim: SYF cells lacking Src, Yes, and Fyn exhibit strong clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol after EGF stimulation.
source: As in NIH3T3 cells, SYF cells exhibited strong clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol after stimulation with EGF (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1I-J showing ZtSH2 clearance in SYF cells comparable to NIH3T3 cells.

claim: SFK-mediated phosphorylation is not required for pYtag function.
source: Combined with the rapid responses observed after EGFR stimulation and inhibition (Figure 1C–E), these results suggest that the EGFR pYtag acts as a direct biosensor of EGFR activity.
evidence: Inferred from data in Figure 1I-J showing pYtag function in SYF cells lacking SFKs, combined with rapid kinetics data.

claim: The EGFR pYtag acts as a direct biosensor of EGFR activity.
source: Combined with the rapid responses observed after EGFR stimulation and inhibition (Figure 1C–E), these results suggest that the EGFR pYtag acts as a direct biosensor of EGFR activity.
evidence: Inferred from rapid kinetics (Figure 1C-E) and SFK-independence (Figure 1I-J).

claim: Cells with higher EGFR expression show greater ZtSH2 redistribution when ZtSH2 levels are similar.
source: When comparing cells with similar levels of ZtSH2 but different levels of EGFR, we observed a greater degree of ZtSH2 redistribution in cells with higher EGFR expression (Figure 1—figure supplements 2A and 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplements 2A and 3A showing correlation between EGFR expression and ZtSH2 clearance.

claim: Cells with lower ZtSH2 expression show more complete ZtSH2 clearance when EGFR levels are similar.
source: Conversely, imaging cells with similar levels of EGFR but different levels of ZtSH2 revealed more complete ZtSH2 clearance in cells with lower ZtSH2 expression (Figure 1—figure supplements 2B and 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplements 2B and 3B showing inverse correlation between ZtSH2 expression and clearance extent.

claim: Higher EGFR:ZtSH2 expression ratios result in consistently higher degrees of ZtSH2 clearance.
source: More broadly, quantifying cytosolic ZtSH2 clearance across all cells revealed consistently higher degrees of ZtSH2 clearance in cells with a high EGFR:ZtSH2 expression ratio, as measured by the ratio of their fluorescence intensities prior to stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplements 2C,D and 3C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplements 2C-D and 3C-D showing correlation between EGFR:ZtSH2 ratio and clearance amplitude.

claim: A mathematical model predicts that ZtSH2 translocation percentage varies linearly with EGFR-to-ZtSH2 ratio until saturation.
source: This phenomenon was also matched by a simplified mathematical model of EGFR activation and ZtSH2 redistribution (see text for Figure 3 and 'Methods' for a detailed discussion of the model), where the percentage translocation of ZtSH2 varied linearly with the EGFR-to-ZtSH2 ratio until it saturated under conditions where the amount of ZtSH2 exceeded that of active EGFR (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The EGFR:ZtSH2 ratio sets the dynamic range of the pYtag translocation-based biosensor.
source: In sum, these results suggest that a simple ratio – the amount of ITAM-tagged EGFR relative to the amount of cytoplasmic ZtSH2 – sets the dynamic range of this translocation-based biosensor.
evidence: Inferred from data in Figure 1—figure supplements 2-4 showing relationship between expression ratio and response amplitude.

claim: Response kinetics of the pYtag biosensor are similarly rapid at all EGFR:ZtSH2 expression levels.
source: While steady-state ZtSH2 cytosolic clearance depended on the EGFR:ZtSH2 ratio, we observed similarly rapid activation kinetics at all expression levels.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplements 2F and 3F showing normalized kinetics are similar across expression levels.

claim: The pYtag biosensor faithfully reports on the kinetics of RTK activation across a range of component expression levels.
source: These results suggest that the pYtag biosensor approach faithfully reports on the kinetics of RTK activation across a range of component expression levels, but that response amplitude should be compared only between cells at similar expression levels of both the ITAM-tagged RTK and fluorescent ZtSH2 probe.
evidence: Inferred from data in Figure 1—figure supplements 2-4 showing consistent kinetics but variable amplitude across expression levels.

claim: ZtSH2 is cleared from the cytosol in a biphasic manner after EGF treatment, with an initial rapid phase within ~40 seconds followed by a gradual increase over ~20 minutes.
source: We found that ZtSH2 was cleared from the cytosol in a biphasic manner, with an initial phase of rapid cytosolic clearance occurring within the first ~40 s, followed by a further gradual increase in cytosolic clearance over the subsequent ~20 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A-B showing timelapse imaging and quantification of biphasic ZtSH2 clearance kinetics.

claim: Sustained ZtSH2 translocation to the membrane persists for at least 30 minutes after EGF stimulation.
source: We observed sustained ZtSH2 translocation to the membrane for at least 30 min, indicating that high levels of membrane-localized, active EGFR are persistent at the membrane under these conditions (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A timelapse images showing continued ZtSH2 membrane localization at 23:20 min.

claim: Similar biphasic responses for EGFR were observed previously at the population-level using a split luciferase system.
source: Similar biphasic responses for EGFR were observed previously at the population-level using a split luciferase system (Macdonald-Obermann and Pike, 2014; Macdonald-Obermann et al., 2012) and in vitro for EGFR on synthetic vesicles (Kovacs et al., 2015), but have never been reported for individual cells.
evidence: Cited from prior literature with references to Macdonald-Obermann and Pike, 2014; Macdonald-Obermann et al., 2012; Kovacs et al., 2015.

claim: Biphasic EGFR responses have never been reported for individual cells prior to this study.
source: Similar biphasic responses for EGFR were observed previously at the population-level using a split luciferase system (Macdonald-Obermann and Pike, 2014; Macdonald-Obermann et al., 2012) and in vitro for EGFR on synthetic vesicles (Kovacs et al., 2015), but have never been reported for individual cells.
evidence: Stated explicitly with citations showing prior work was at population level or in vitro.

claim: NIH3T3 cells retain high levels of membrane-associated EGFR for at least 60 minutes after EGF stimulation.
source: Quantifying EGFR membrane intensity revealed that cells retain high levels of membrane-associated EGFR for at least 60 min after EGF stimulation, and that this response is independent of whether our pYtag components are present (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C showing sustained membrane EGFR levels over 60 minutes.

claim: Membrane-associated EGFR levels are independent of whether pYtag components are present.
source: Quantifying EGFR membrane intensity revealed that cells retain high levels of membrane-associated EGFR for at least 60 min after EGF stimulation, and that this response is independent of whether our pYtag components are present (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C comparing control and pYtag-expressing cells.

claim: pYtag-expressing cells stimulated with EGF contain puncta that are positive for both total EGFR and ZtSH2.
source: Despite sustained, high levels of membrane-localized EGFR, we also observed that pYtag-expressing cells stimulated with EGF contained puncta that were positive for both total EGFR and ZtSH2 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2C-D showing puncta containing both EGFR and ZtSH2.

claim: Puncta containing EGFR, ZtSH2, and EEA1 colocalize in both NIH3T3 and HEK293T cells after EGF stimulation.
source: Co-staining cells at various time points after EGF stimulation for the early endocytic marker EEA1 revealed colocalization between puncta containing EGFR, ZtSH2, and EEA1 in both NIH3T3 and HEK293T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-G showing immunostaining colocalization.

claim: Gefitinib treatment rapidly eliminates ZtSH2 from EGFR-positive puncta.
source: Furthermore, subsequent treatment with gefitinib rapidly eliminated ZtSH2 from EGFR-positive puncta, suggesting that the enrichment of ZtSH2 at puncta is indicative of signaling from endosomal compartments (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2C-D showing loss of ZtSH2 from puncta after gefitinib treatment.

claim: The enrichment of ZtSH2 at puncta is indicative of signaling from endosomal compartments.
source: Furthermore, subsequent treatment with gefitinib rapidly eliminated ZtSH2 from EGFR-positive puncta, suggesting that the enrichment of ZtSH2 at puncta is indicative of signaling from endosomal compartments (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Inferred from colocalization with EEA1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-G) and gefitinib-reversibility (Figure 2C-D).

claim: Internalized EGFR remains bound to its ligand and can transmit signals from endosomal compartments.
source: These results are consistent with prior reports that internalized EGFR remains bound to its ligand and can transmit signals from endosomal compartments (Haugh et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Haugh et al., 1999) and consistent with current observations.

claim: EGFR-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells retain a high degree of membrane-associated receptor signaling for at least 1 hour after EGF stimulation.
source: Nevertheless, we find that EGFR-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells retain a high degree of membrane-associated receptor signaling for at least 1 hr after EGF stimulation.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B showing sustained membrane EGFR.

claim: MCF10A cells form multicellular clusters when cultured on soft substrata.
source: We previously found that MCF10A human mammary epithelial cells form multicellular clusters when cultured on soft substrata and exhibit a complex spatial pattern of EGF binding at cell membranes (Farahani et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Farahani et al., 2021) and illustrated in Figure 2E-F.

claim: EGF binds rapidly to media-exposed membranes on the surface of MCF10A clusters but is excluded from lateral membranes and interior cells.
source: Measurements of fixed tissues revealed that EGF binds rapidly to the media-exposed membranes on the surface of the cluster but is excluded from lateral membranes and from cells located within the interior of the cluster (Farahani et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from prior work (Farahani et al., 2021).

claim: MCF10A cells cultured on soft substrata exhibit a radially directed wave of EGFR and Erk signaling after EGF treatment.
source: We treated MCF10A cells cultured on soft substrata with EGF and observed a radially directed wave of EGFR and Erk signaling: activation first appeared in cells at the periphery of the clusters before appearing in cells at the interior (Figure 2F, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2F timelapse images and Figure 2H heatmaps showing spatial progression of signaling.

claim: In peripheral MCF10A cells, ZtSH2 is first enriched at the media-exposed membrane before localizing to lateral membranes.
source: In cells at the periphery of clusters, we found that ZtSH2 was first enriched at the media-exposed membrane before localizing to lateral membranes (Figure 2G), highlighting the differences in receptor-level signaling between membrane subcompartments.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2G line scans showing temporal sequence of ZtSH2 enrichment at different membrane locations.

claim: There is a 2-4 minute delay in EGFR and Erk signaling between the periphery and interior of MCF10A clusters.
source: Quantifying EGFR and Erk responses confirmed our qualitative observations, revealing a 2–4 min delay in EGFR and Erk signaling between the periphery and interior of clusters (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2H-I showing time to half maximal response differences between peripheral and interior cells.

claim: Erk responses trail EGFR responses by approximately 4 minutes.
source: Notably, Erk responses also trailed those of EGFR by ~4 min, consistent with the delay in signal transmission previously observed from Ras to Erk (Figure 2J; Toettcher et al., 2013).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2J and consistent with prior literature (Toettcher et al., 2013).

claim: Ligand-receptor interactions are limited at cell-cell contacts, producing an inward-traveling wave of RTK activation and downstream signaling.
source: These data support a model in which ligand–receptor interactions are limited at cell–cell contacts, producing an inward-traveling wave of RTK activation and downstream signaling.
evidence: Inferred from spatial and temporal patterns shown in Figure 2F-J.

claim: pYtags can reveal RTK signaling dynamics at high temporal resolution and over both subcellular and multicellular length scales.
source: More broadly, our data demonstrate that pYtags can be used to reveal RTK signaling dynamics at high temporal resolution and over both subcellular and multicellular length scales.
evidence: Demonstrated across Figures 2A-J showing subcellular (membrane subcompartments) and multicellular (cluster) measurements.

claim: High-affinity EGFR ligands such as EGF produce long-lived EGFR dimers that are internalized and degraded.
source: For instance, high-affinity EGFR ligands such as EGF produce long-lived EGFR dimers that are internalized and degraded, whereas low-affinity ligands such as epiregulin (EREG) and epigen (EPGN) produce shorter-lived EGFR dimers that prolong signaling, leading to distinct cell-fate outcomes (Freed et al., 2017; Roepstorff et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Freed et al., 2017; Roepstorff et al., 2009).

claim: Low-affinity ligands such as EREG and EPGN produce shorter-lived EGFR dimers that prolong signaling, leading to distinct cell-fate outcomes.
source: For instance, high-affinity EGFR ligands such as EGF produce long-lived EGFR dimers that are internalized and degraded, whereas low-affinity ligands such as epiregulin (EREG) and epigen (EPGN) produce shorter-lived EGFR dimers that prolong signaling, leading to distinct cell-fate outcomes (Freed et al., 2017; Roepstorff et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Freed et al., 2017; Roepstorff et al., 2009).

claim: EGF treatment produces a gradual rise in EGFR activity at lower doses (0.2-2 ng/mL).
source: For EGF, we observed a gradual rise in activity at lower doses (0.2–2 ng/mL). This response switched to a biphasic response at higher doses (5–100 ng/mL), with a rapid initial phase in first 1–2 min followed by a slower, continued rise (Figure 3A, left panel).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3A left panel showing dose-dependent kinetics for EGF.

claim: EGF treatment produces a biphasic response at higher doses (5-100 ng/mL), with a rapid initial phase in the first 1-2 minutes followed by a slower, continued rise.
source: For EGF, we observed a gradual rise in activity at lower doses (0.2–2 ng/mL). This response switched to a biphasic response at higher doses (5–100 ng/mL), with a rapid initial phase in first 1–2 min followed by a slower, continued rise (Figure 3A, left panel).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3A left panel showing biphasic kinetics at high EGF doses.

claim: Treatment with EREG and EPGN produces a small transient peak of EGFR activation shortly after stimulation, indicative of a weakly adaptive response.
source: We also observed a small but reproducible transient peak of EGFR activation shortly after treatment with EREG and EPGN but not with EGF, indicative of a weakly adaptive response after stimulation with low-affinity ligands (Figure 3A, middle and right panels).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3A middle and right panels showing transient peak for EREG/EPGN but not EGF.

claim: Different EGFR ligands produce markedly different signaling responses in the first few minutes following stimulation.
source: These results demonstrate that different ligands produce markedly different signaling responses even in the first few minutes following stimulation.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3A showing distinct kinetics for EGF vs EREG/EPGN.

claim: Altering concentrations of low-affinity ligands EREG and EPGN has a strong effect on the amplitude, but not the kinetics, of EGFR activation.
source: They also reveal an unusual property of the low-affinity RTK ligands EREG and EPGN: altering their concentrations has a strong effect on the amplitude, but not the kinetics, of EGFR activation.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3A middle and right panels showing dose-dependent amplitude but similar kinetics for EREG/EPGN.

claim: A mathematical model of EGFR pYtag was constructed based on mass-action kinetics including ligand binding, receptor dimerization/autophosphorylation, and ZtSH2 recruitment.
source: To begin addressing this question, we constructed a simplified mathematical model of the EGFR pYtag system based on mass-action kinetics that could be used to interrogate differences between ligands (Figure 3B). In our model, EGFR monomers can bind ligands, dimerize, undergo autophosphorylation and, lastly, bind to ZtSH2.
evidence: Described in text and illustrated in Figure 3B schematic.

claim: The mathematical model includes pre-formed EGFR dimers in the absence of ligand.
source: We also modeled pre-formed EGFR dimers in the absence of ligand, based on several observations of these inactive dimers (Bessman et al., 2014; Moriki et al., 2001; Yu et al., 2002; Saffarian et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Bessman et al., 2014; Moriki et al., 2001; Yu et al., 2002; Saffarian et al., 2007).

claim: Endocytosis and trafficking were neglected in the mathematical model based on observations that EGFR-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells maintain a large, constant pool of membrane-localized EGFR.
source: We chose to neglect endocytosis and trafficking in our model based on observations that our EGFR-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells maintain a large, constant pool of membrane-localized EGFR in each of our experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Justified by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing sustained membrane EGFR.

claim: Decreasing the dimerization affinity of ligand-bound receptors (increasing γ) is sufficient to reproduce EREG/EPGN-like features including an initial peak followed by a plateau.
source: Decreasing the dimerization affinity of ligand-bound receptors by increasing γ was sufficient to reproduce many of the features that varied with ligand identity. Simulations with γ = 100 produced an EREG/EPGN-like initial peak of receptor activation followed by a plateau (Figure 3C, lower panels).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3C lower panels showing model simulations with increased γ.

claim: Simulating a large change in ligand binding affinity (β = 1000) is unable to qualitatively alter EGFR response kinetics.
source: In contrast, simulating even a very large change in ligand binding affinity (β = 1000) was unable to qualitatively alter response kinetics (Figure 3C, right panel).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3C right panel showing model simulations with increased β.

claim: Differences in receptor dimerization affinity between EGFR ligands play an important role in regulating receptor activation kinetics.
source: In sum, our simulations suggest that differences in receptor dimerization affinity between EGFR ligands could play an important role in regulating receptor activation kinetics.
evidence: Inferred from modeling results in Figure 3C showing γ but not β affects kinetics.

claim: GBM-associated mutations R84K and A265V drive an approximately 650-fold increase in the dimerization affinity of EREG- and EPGN-bound receptors with only a 6-fold change to ligand-receptor binding.
source: We turned to glioblastoma multiform (GBM)-associated mutations in the extracellular domain of EGFR (R84K and A265V point mutations), which were recently shown to drive an ~650-fold increase in the dimerization affinity of EREG- and EPGN-bound receptors with only a 6-fold change to ligand-receptor binding (Hu et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Hu et al., 2022).

claim: The mathematical model predicts that GBM-associated mutants will exhibit a stronger, more gradual signaling response compared to wild-type EGFR in response to 20 ng/mL EREG.
source: We first simulated these GBM-associated mutations in response to 20 ng/mL EREG, which led to the prediction of a stronger, more gradual signaling response in GBM-associated mutants compared to the wild-type receptor, reminiscent of the difference between EGF and EREG responses (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3D showing model predictions for GBM mutants.

claim: Cells expressing GBM-associated EGFR mutants (R84K or A265V) exhibit a stronger response that gradually increases over time when treated with 20 ng/mL EREG.
source: Treating these cells with 20 ng/mL EREG produced signaling responses that closely matched the predictions of our model: cells expressing WT EGFR exhibited a transient peak of activation and rapid plateau, while cells expressing GBM-associated mutants exhibited a stronger response that gradually increased over time (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3E showing experimental validation of model predictions for GBM mutants.

claim: Dimerization affinity of ligand-bound EGFR is a key parameter that governs receptor activation.
source: Taken together, these data support the utility of the pYtag biosensor system for quantitatively studying the dynamics of receptor activation. Furthermore, our results suggest that dimerization affinity of ligand-bound EGFR is a key parameter that governs receptor activation.
evidence: Inferred from modeling (Figure 3C) and experimental validation (Figure 3E) showing dimerization affinity affects kinetics.

claim: ErbB2 is a ligandless receptor that can only be activated in conjunction with an additional ErbB family member such as EGFR.
source: ErbB2 is a ligandless receptor and is particularly challenging to study because it can only be activated in conjunction with an additional ErbB family member such as EGFR (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010) and established knowledge about ErbB2.

claim: General RTK biosensors such as those based on Grb2 are unable to report specifically on ErbB2 activation dynamics due to the obligate presence of a second RTK.
source: As a result, general RTK biosensors such as those based on Grb2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) are unable to report specifically on ErbB2 activation dynamics due to the obligate presence of a second RTK (e.g., EGFR) in the same cells.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for ErbB2 to heterodimerize and the non-specificity of Grb2 shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: pYtags can be used to monitor the activity of FGFR1, PDGFRβ, VEGFR3, and ErbB2.
source: We found that pYtags generalized well across all RTKs tested. Stimulating ErbB2 pYtag-expressing cells with EGF led to clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol, a response that required both the presence of ITAMs on ErbB2 and co-expression of EGFR (Figure 4B and C). Similarly, stimulating FGFR1, PDGFRβ, and VEGFR3 pYtag-expressing cells with their cognate ligands induced cytosolic clearance of ZtSH2, which did not take place in cells that expressed the ITAM-less variants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4B-C for ErbB2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for FGFR1, PDGFRβ, and VEGFR3.

claim: ErbB2 pYtag response to EGF requires both the presence of ITAMs on ErbB2 and co-expression of EGFR.
source: Stimulating ErbB2 pYtag-expressing cells with EGF led to clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol, a response that required both the presence of ITAMs on ErbB2 and co-expression of EGFR (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4B-C showing ZtSH2 clearance only when both ITAMs and EGFR are present.

claim: The pYtag approach is modular and can be readily adapted for monitoring the activation of distinct RTKs in individual cells.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that the pYtag approach is indeed modular and can be readily adapted for monitoring the activation of distinct RTKs in individual cells.
evidence: Demonstrated across multiple RTKs in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ZAP70 phosphorylates non-ITAM tyrosine residues on the scaffold protein SLP76 following its binding to phosphorylated ITAMs on the TCR.
source: Following its binding to phosphorylated ITAMs on the TCR, ZAP70 phosphorylates non-ITAM tyrosine residues on the scaffold protein SLP76, which subsequently recruit multiple signaling components via SH2-mediated interactions (Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014; Weiss and Littman, 1994).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014; Weiss and Littman, 1994).

claim: Tyrosine residues Y128 and Y145 of SLP76, when phosphorylated, bind to SH2 domains from Vav and ITK, respectively.
source: We identified two tyrosine residues of SLP76, Y128 and Y145, which when phosphorylated bind to SH2 domains from the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Vav and the kinase ITK, respectively (Figure 5A; Raab et al., 1997; Koretzky et al., 2006; Su et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Raab et al., 1997; Koretzky et al., 2006; Su et al., 1999) and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: VISH2 is a synthetic tSH2 created by fusing the SH2 domains of Vav and ITK with a 10 bp glycine-serine linker.
source: To create a synthetic tSH2 that could bind tightly to the Y128/Y145 motif, we fused the SH2 domains of Vav and ITK together with a 10 bp glycine-serine linker to create VISH2.
evidence: Described explicitly in the text.

claim: Cells expressing SLP76-labeled EGFR exhibit clearance of VISH2 from the cytosol but no crosstalk with ZtSH2 upon EGF stimulation.
source: Stimulating the two cell lines with EGF and monitoring the localization of VISH2 and ZtSH2 revealed that cells expressing SLP76-labeled EGFR exhibited clearance of VISH2 from the cytosol but no crosstalk with ZtSH2 (Figure 5B–D, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5B-D showing selective VISH2 clearance without ZtSH2 response.

claim: Cells expressing CD3ε-labeled EGFR exhibit strong clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol with minimal crosstalk with VISH2 upon EGF stimulation.
source: Conversely, cells expressing CD3ε-labeled EGFR exhibited strong clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol with minimal crosstalk with VISH2 (Figure 5B–D, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5B-D showing selective ZtSH2 clearance without VISH2 response.

claim: The VISH2/SLP76 and CD3ε/ZtSH2 pYtags operate independently of one another to report the activity of EGFR.
source: The VISH2/SLP76 and CD3ε/ZtSH2 pYtags thus operate independently of one another to report the activity of EGFR.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5B-D showing orthogonal responses of the two pYtag systems.

claim: Both VISH2 and ZtSH2 reporters clear from the cytosol when cells co-expressing EGFR and ErbB2 pYtags are treated with EGF.
source: We treated cells with 100 ng/mL EGF and observed that both VISH2 and ZtSH2 reporters cleared from the cytosol, as would be expected from the activation of EGFR and ErbB2 heterodimers.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5F-H showing clearance of both reporters.

claim: VISH2 clears from the cytosol almost immediately (<30 seconds) after EGF treatment in cells co-expressing EGFR and ErbB2 pYtags.
source: VISH2 cleared from the cytosol almost immediately (<30 s), indicating rapid phosphorylation of the EGFR C-terminal tail.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5F-H showing rapid VISH2 clearance kinetics.

claim: ZtSH2 exhibits a more gradual clearance from the cytosol (~3 minutes) after EGF treatment in cells co-expressing EGFR and ErbB2 pYtags.
source: In contrast, ZtSH2 exhibited a more gradual clearance from the cytosol (~3 min), suggesting a delay in ErbB2 phosphorylation.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5F-H showing slower ZtSH2 clearance kinetics compared to VISH2.

claim: The dynamics of EGFR and ErbB2 activation are tightly overlapping when normalized to maximum response amplitude, irrespective of the cell line or pYtag used.
source: However, when normalized to their maximum response amplitude, the dynamics of EGFR and ErbB2 activation were tightly overlapping in all cases, irrespective of the cell line or pYtag used (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C showing consistent normalized kinetics across conditions.

claim: pYtag measurements faithfully reflect the activity dynamics of the RTK on which they report.
source: These data provide further evidence that pYtag measurements faithfully reflect the activity dynamics of the RTK on which they report.
evidence: Inferred from consistent dynamics across different pYtag variants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: EGFR is activated first, within seconds of EGF stimulation, and then both EGFR and ErbB2 are further activated over the subsequent minutes.
source: Moreover, our results suggest that EGFR and ErbB2 are activated in distinct phases: EGFR is activated first, within seconds of stimulation, and then both EGFR and ErbB2 are further activated over the subsequent minutes.
evidence: Inferred from differential kinetics shown in Figure 5F-H where EGFR responds faster than ErbB2.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing was used to label the C-terminus of endogenous EGFR with three repeats of the CD3ε ITAM and mNeonGreen in HEK293T cells.
source: We used CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing to label the C-terminus of endogenous EGFR with three repeats of the CD3ε ITAM and a fluorescent protein via homology-directed repair (HDR) in HEK293T cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: Described in text and illustrated in Figure 6A schematic.

claim: Genomic integration of CD3ε-mNeonGreen at the endogenous EGFR locus was verified by PCR of genomic DNA.
source: We sorted an mNeonGreen-expressing clonal cell line and confirmed proper labeling of EGFR with CD3ε-mNeonGreen by PCR of genomic DNA (Figure 6B) and immunoblotting of cell lysates (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B showing PCR validation of genomic integration.

claim: Expression of EGFR-CD3ε-mNeonGreen protein was verified by immunoblotting.
source: We sorted an mNeonGreen-expressing clonal cell line and confirmed proper labeling of EGFR with CD3ε-mNeonGreen by PCR of genomic DNA (Figure 6B) and immunoblotting of cell lysates (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6C showing immunoblot validation of protein expression.

claim: EGFR-pYtag knock-in HEK293T cells exhibit rapid clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol following EGF treatment.
source: The resulting EGFR-pYtag knock-in HEK293T cells exhibited rapid clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol following EGF treatment, whereas no ZtSH2 response was observed in parental cells (Figure 6D–F, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6D-F showing ZtSH2 clearance in knock-in but not parental cells.

claim: Parental HEK293T cells show no ZtSH2 response to EGF treatment.
source: The resulting EGFR-pYtag knock-in HEK293T cells exhibited rapid clearance of ZtSH2 from the cytosol following EGF treatment, whereas no ZtSH2 response was observed in parental cells (Figure 6D–F, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6D-F showing no ZtSH2 clearance in parental cells.

claim: pYtags can be used to monitor the activation state of endogenously expressed RTKs.
source: We therefore conclude that pYtags can be used to monitor the activation state of endogenously expressed RTKs, opening the door to single-cell studies of RTK signaling dynamics and endocytic trafficking in minimally perturbed contexts.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6D-F showing functional pYtag in CRISPR knock-in cells.

claim: EGFR-pYtag knock-in cells show a decrease in ZtSH2 membrane localization within minutes after EGF stimulation.
source: For our EGFR-pYtag knock-in cells, we observed a decrease in ZtSH2 membrane localization within minutes after EGF stimulation, as well as near-complete loss of endogenous EGFR from the cell membrane within 8 min, with some internalized puncta that retained ZtSH2 labeling, likely reflecting internalization (Figure 6D, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6D and Figure 6—video 1 showing temporal dynamics of ZtSH2 and EGFR.

claim: Endogenous EGFR shows near-complete loss from the cell membrane within 8 minutes after EGF stimulation in knock-in cells.
source: For our EGFR-pYtag knock-in cells, we observed a decrease in ZtSH2 membrane localization within minutes after EGF stimulation, as well as near-complete loss of endogenous EGFR from the cell membrane within 8 min, with some internalized puncta that retained ZtSH2 labeling, likely reflecting internalization (Figure 6D, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6D and Figure 6—video 1 showing EGFR internalization.

claim: HEK293T cells ectopically expressing high levels of EGFR-pYtag retain EGFR at the membrane for at least 10 minutes after EGF stimulation.
source: In comparison, HEK293T cells ectopically expressing high levels of an identical EGFR-pYtag system retained EGFR at the membrane for at least 10 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B showing sustained membrane EGFR in overexpressing cells.

claim: EGFR endocytosis can be saturated at high levels of receptor expression.
source: These data are in agreement with prior reports that EGFR endocytosis can be saturated at high levels of receptor expression (Lund et al., 1990) and suggest that the pYtag strategy might be useful in future studies to relate EGFR activity, internalization, and trafficking at high resolution in single cells.
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Lund et al., 1990) and consistent with current observations comparing knock-in vs overexpressing cells.

claim: pYtags quantitatively report on RTK activity with sub-minute temporal precision.
source: pYtags quantitatively report on RTK activity with sub-minute temporal precision and can be applied to monitor signaling at both subcellular and multicellular length scales.
evidence: Demonstrated throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2 and 3 showing rapid kinetics.

claim: pYtag responses are highly reproducible across multiple experiments and independently derived cell lines.
source: Responses are highly reproducible across multiple experiments and independently derived cell lines, even when the same receptor is monitored using different pYtag variants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing consistent responses across conditions.

claim: pYtags are modular and can be applied to multiple RTKs without modification.
source: First, pYtags are modular: they can be applied to multiple RTKs without modification, unlike approaches that seek to identify phosphotyrosine/SH2 interactions present on endogenous RTKs (Tiruthani et al., 2019).
evidence: Demonstrated across Figures 4 and 4—figure supplement 1 showing application to multiple RTKs.

claim: pYtags are specific, reporting only on the activity of the RTK labeled by the tyrosine activation motif.
source: Second, pYtags are specific, reporting only on the activity of the RTK labeled by the tyrosine activation motif.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1D-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing specificity for ITAM-tagged receptors.

claim: pYtags require one fewer fluorescent protein compared to FRET-based biosensors.
source: Third, pYtags can be multiplexed: these biosensors require one fewer fluorescent protein compared to FRET-based biosensors, and orthogonal variants of pYtags can be used to monitor distinct RTKs in the same cell.
evidence: Stated explicitly and demonstrated in Figure 5 showing multiplexed biosensors.

claim: Orthogonal variants of pYtags can be used to monitor distinct RTKs in the same cell.
source: Third, pYtags can be multiplexed: these biosensors require one fewer fluorescent protein compared to FRET-based biosensors, and orthogonal variants of pYtags can be used to monitor distinct RTKs in the same cell.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5 showing simultaneous monitoring of EGFR and ErbB2.

claim: The human genome encodes at least 58 RTKs.
source: The human genome encodes at least 58 RTKs (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010), most of which remain poorly characterized with respect to their spatial organization and signaling dynamics.
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).

claim: Most RTKs remain poorly characterized with respect to their spatial organization and signaling dynamics.
source: The human genome encodes at least 58 RTKs (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010), most of which remain poorly characterized with respect to their spatial organization and signaling dynamics.
evidence: Stated explicitly with citation to Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010.

claim: pYtags require a tyrosine activation motif to be appended to an RTK of interest, necessitating either ectopic expression or direct genome editing.
source: First, pYtags require a tyrosine activation motif to be appended to an RTK of interest, necessitating either ectopic expression of the labeled receptor or direct genome editing of the endogenous receptor.
evidence: Stated explicitly as a limitation of the approach.

claim: pYtags are currently restricted to nonimmune cells that do not endogenously express the corresponding immune signaling proteins.
source: A second limitation of pYtags is its reliance on phosphotyrosine/tSH2 motifs from immune signaling proteins. As a result, pYtags are currently restricted to nonimmune cells that do not endogenously express the corresponding proteins.
evidence: Stated explicitly as a limitation based on the source of the components.

claim: NIH3T3 cells express very low levels of endogenous EGFR.
source: We co-expressed each receptor with an iRFP-labeled ZtSH2 (iRFP-ZtSH2) in NIH3T3 fibroblasts (Figure 1B), which express very low levels of endogenous EGFR (Di Fiore et al., 1987; Livneh et al., 1986; Eierhoff et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Di Fiore et al., 1987; Livneh et al., 1986; Eierhoff et al., 2010).

claim: ZtSH2 binds 100-fold more tightly to ITAMs than individual ZAP70 SH2 domains.
source: During activation of the T-cell receptor (TCR), pairs of tyrosine residues located in immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) are phosphorylated and serve as sites for the selective recruitment of the tandem SH2 domain of ZAP70 (ZtSH2), which binds 100-fold more tightly than individual ZAP70 SH2 domains with the same ITAMs and displays minimal crosstalk with other phosphotyrosine-containing peptides (Figure 1A; Isakov et al., 1995; Labadia et al., 1996; Wange et al., 1993).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Isakov et al., 1995; Labadia et al., 1996; Wange et al., 1993).

claim: ZtSH2 displays minimal crosstalk with other phosphotyrosine-containing peptides.
source: During activation of the T-cell receptor (TCR), pairs of tyrosine residues located in immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) are phosphorylated and serve as sites for the selective recruitment of the tandem SH2 domain of ZAP70 (ZtSH2), which binds 100-fold more tightly than individual ZAP70 SH2 domains with the same ITAMs and displays minimal crosstalk with other phosphotyrosine-containing peptides (Figure 1A; Isakov et al., 1995; Labadia et al., 1996; Wange et al., 1993).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Isakov et al., 1995; Labadia et al., 1996; Wange et al., 1993).

claim: Neither the TCR nor ZAP70 are expressed by nonimmune cells.
source: Because neither the TCR nor ZAP70 are expressed by nonimmune cells, we reasoned that an ITAM/ZtSH2 pair may be repurposed as an orthogonal interaction module to monitor the activity of a desired RTK in nonimmune contexts.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about immune-specific protein expression.
